Ryan: Yeah, I can hear you.
Joanne: Oh good, thank goodness. I'm Joanne, I'm in Gosport, down near Portsmouth. Erm, I don't really know what we're meant to talk about, do you?
Ryan: Not really. Just chat, I think. I'm Ryan. Castleford.
Joanne: Castleford, is that up north, love?
Ryan: Yeah, West Yorkshire. Near Wakefield.
Joanne: Oh lovely. I've never been up that way, I don't get about much, I sort of stay local. What do you do, if you don't mind me asking?
Ryan: Mechanic. Small independent garage. Servicing, brakes, MOTs and that.
Joanne: Oh, that's ever so handy. My sister Michelle's always saying she wants someone she can trust with her car. She had her clutch done last year and she was convinced they ripped her off, you know, she came round mine nearly in tears about it.
Ryan: Happens a lot, to be fair. Clutch is a big job though. It's mostly labour. What'd she pay?
Joanne: Erm, I think it was about six hundred?
Ryan: Bit steep. Not mad though. Depends on the car.
Joanne: Well, that's made me feel better for her, I'll tell her that. Sorry, I'm rabbiting on. Do you like it, the job?
Ryan: It's alright. Pays the bills. Mostly. Mad busy at the minute, everyone's MOTs are due at once.
Joanne: Oh I bet. I work in a school kitchen, a primary. Eleven years now. Food prep, serving at lunchtime, washing up, wiping down the hall after. I know all the kiddies, which ones have allergies, which ones won't touch a pea. There's one little boy who'll pick every single pea out and line them up on the side of his plate, bless him.
Ryan: Ha. My girlfriend works at a nursery. She says same. Kids and food.
Joanne: Oh does she? Ah, that's nice. What's her name?
Ryan: Chloe. She likes it. Knackered all the time though.
Joanne: Oh, I know that feeling. My knees are terrible on cold mornings, I sort of creak in through the door.
Ryan: I'm on me feet all day an' all. Under cars. Back's not great.
Joanne: Oh, you're too young for a bad back, love! Erm, what did you make of that puzzle thing at the start? I was useless. I love a jigsaw, but that one, I just went to pieces.
Ryan: Didn't finish it. Ran out of time.
Joanne: Oh, thank goodness, I thought it was just me.
Ryan: Do you do jigsaws then?
Joanne: Oh, all the time. Thousand-piece ones, countryside scenes mostly. The one I've got on the go now is a nightmare, it's all sky, just blue and more blue. And my cat Biscuit likes to sit right in the middle of it, so I'm forever lifting him off and finding bits stuck to his fur.
Ryan: We've got a dog. Bruno. He'd eat a jigsaw. He chewed one of Chloe's shoes last week.
Joanne: Oh no! Was she cross?
Ryan: Bit. It were a new one. He weren't bothered.
Joanne: They never are, are they? Biscuit knocked my tea over Tuesday and just looked at me. Erm, what do you do of an evening then, after work?
Ryan: Walk the dog. Have me tea. PlayStation. That's about it really.
Joanne: That sounds nice and quiet. I have my dinner and put The Chase on, that's my evening. I don't know if that's very exciting, sorry.
Ryan: Me mam watches that. Shouts at it.
Joanne: Oh, I shout at it too! Don't tell anyone. Does your mam get many right?
Ryan: More than me, to be fair.

=== CALL C0571 ===

Tracey: Tracey. Sittingbourne.

Gemma: Five! Gosh. I'm a speech and language therapist. Self-employed now, mostly after-school clients and a Saturday morning. Before that I did about ten years in NHS community paediatrics, so, you know, I know the system inside out.
Tracey: Right. So kids that can't talk properly?
Gemma: Well, sort of. It's more speech sound delays, language delays, kids who are behind with putting sentences together. It's not just "can't talk", yeah?
Tracey: My sister's youngest had something like that. Waited about a year on the NHS.
Gemma: Yeah, that's the problem, the waiting lists are shocking. That's partly why people come private.
Tracey: Couldn't afford private, to be honest.
Gemma: No, I get that, it isn't cheap. Erm, so do you like the early shifts?
Tracey: Love finishing at eleven. Rest of the day's mine. Getting up at quarter past four's the killer.
Gemma: I'd be knackered. I'm out at parkrun Saturdays if I haven't got clients, and even that feels early.
Tracey: Running for fun? No thanks. I walk the dog round the rec, that'll do me.
Gemma: What have you got?
Tracey: Staffie. Roxy. She's old now, dodgy hips. The vet bills are something else.
Gemma: Oh bless her. My son Alfie's desperate for a dog, but Dean says absolutely not.
Tracey: My other half's Dean.
Gemma: No way! What does yours do?
Tracey: Scaffolder. Self-employed.
Gemma: Mine's an electrician, got his own little business. He leaves the van on the drive at this ridiculous angle every single night and it drives me up the wall, I've told him a hundred times.
Tracey: That's every bloke with a van. Ours broke down again last week, I had to go and fetch him from Faversham.
Gemma: Oh, nightmare. Did you get on alright with that puzzle at the start, by the way?
Tracey: Gave up halfway. Couldn't be bothered.
Gemma: I finished it with about a minute to spare, actually.
Tracey: Course you did.
Gemma: Sorry, what's that supposed to mean?
Tracey: Nothing bad. You just look organised. I saw that calendar behind you with all the colours.
Gemma: Okay, guilty. It's colour-coded by child. Ruby's just started secondary and the homework's ridiculous, so I have to track it or we'd fall apart.
Tracey: Mine's a free one from the Chinese. Says Lucky Garden on it.
Gemma: Ha. Is that your Friday night then?
Tracey: Every Friday. Chicken chow mein, salt and pepper chips. Not changing that.
Gemma: We're a curry family on a Friday. Dean'd riot if I tried to cook.
Tracey: Same. Fridays I'm not doing nothing.

=== CALL C0572 ===

Tracey: Yeah, hear you fine. Tracey, Sittingbourne.
Joanne: Oh, Kent. I nearly said when I saw your picture, you remind me of my sister Michelle. Sorry, is that a strange thing to say?
Tracey: No, it's alright. You remind me of me mum, to be honest, so we're even.

Tracey: Shelf stacking. Supermarket, early mornings. Up at quarter past four, start at five, done at eleven.

Joanne: Oh, love. I know that one. I looked after my mum at the end, she had a long illness, and erm, it was mostly me as well. Michelle helped where she could, but. You know.

Joanne: They do. Sorry, that's a bit heavy for three minutes, isn't it? I don't know if that's what you wanted.

Joanne: Ha! Do you get away much? Holidays and that?

Tracey: Just drive.
Joanne: I don't drive, love! That's half the problem. Erm, what did you make of that puzzle at the beginning?
Tracey: Gave up. Told the woman I had before, she finished it with a minute to spare.
Joanne: Oh, I didn't finish it either. I felt a bit thick, to be honest.
Tracey: You ain't thick. It was just a daft puzzle.
Joanne: Thank you, that's kind. What do you do Friday nights? Mine's fish and chips, my one treat.
Tracey: Chinese. Every week.

=== CALL C0574 ===

Chiamaka: No, that's a good thing! Do you have holidays planned? I need a holiday after these nights.

Gemma: At least you're honest. What do you do to unwind, then?
Chiamaka: Choir at church, I'm an alto, and Love Island. Don't judge me!
Gemma: I wasn't going to judge you. Well, a little bit.
Chiamaka: Ha! Everyone says that, then they're watching it with me by week two!
Gemma: I've got a book group. We're doing a Booker longlist one this month and I'm the only one who's finished it, as usual.
Chiamaka: See, you are the organised one. I knew it from your picture.

=== CALL C0575 ===
Joanne: Hello, love, can you hear me? I'm Joanne, from Gosport.
Shazia: Yeah. Shazia. Walsall.
Joanne: Oh, the Midlands. Erm, I never know how to start these. What do you do, Shazia?
Shazia: Nothing at the minute. I'm at home with the kids. I used to pack at a warehouse but me back went.
Joanne: Oh, I'm sorry. Backs are awful. Mine's not brilliant either, and my knees. I'm a kitchen assistant at a primary school, have been for eleven years.
Shazia: School kitchen? That's what I was thinking of doing. Once my youngest goes up to secondary. Dinner lady or a TA, something in school hours.
Joanne: Oh, you'd be lovely at it! Honestly. It's term-time, so you get the holidays with your kids, that's the big thing.
Shazia: Is it hard on your back, though? To be honest that's what I'm worried about.

Shazia: Most. She's alright. She just sits there and tells me how to do things, d'you know what I mean.
Joanne: Oh dear. Ha. My mum used to do that, God rest her. She'd stand at my cooker going "you want more salt in that".
Shazia: Yeah. That's her.
Joanne: Do you get a bit of time for yourself at all?
Shazia: Dramas. Pakistani dramas on YouTube, at night. I'm hooked on one now, she's just found out her husband's been lying about everything.

Shazia: That's nice, that.
Joanne: Thank you, love. I don't know if that's very interesting.
Shazia: It is. More useful than me watching YouTube.
Joanne: Oh no, we all need our telly. What do they eat at your house for a treat, then?
Shazia: Chips from the chippy on a Friday, in a bap. Hamza won't have it any other way.

=== CALL C0576 ===
Chiamaka: Hello hello! Can you hear me okay? I'm Chiamaka, in Leeds.
Tracey: Yeah. Tracey. Sittingbourne, in Kent.
Chiamaka: Kent! The garden of England, they call it, right? So what do you do, Tracey?
Tracey: Shelf stacking. Early mornings at a supermarket. What about you, you're a nurse or something? I saw the top.
Chiamaka: Doctor, actually! Acute medicine. But honestly, the nurses run the place, I just get the credit, ha. I've just come off four nights so I'm a bit loopy.
Tracey: Four nights. I'm up at quarter past four and I moan about it.
Chiamaka: No, quarter past four is a proper night shift, that counts! You're on your feet the whole time as well, lifting, everything.
Tracey: Yeah. Quicker than most of them, to be honest. I just want it done so I can go home at eleven.
Chiamaka: I love that. Get in, get it done, go home. I wish I could do that, but there's always one more discharge summary.
Tracey: Can I ask you something, since you're a doctor?
Chiamaka: Go on, everyone does! My whole family WhatsApp asks me.
Tracey: My mum's getting forgetful. Like, leaving the gas on, asking the same thing three times. She's had the memory test at the GP and they've referred her, but it's been months. Is that normal, the wait?
Chiamaka: Erm. Honestly? Yeah, the memory clinic waits are long, it's not just you. What I'd say is, if something happens, like a fall, or she gets suddenly confused, really suddenly, over a day or two, that's different, that can be an infection, and you get her seen quickly. Don't wait on the clinic for that. And keep a little list of what you notice, dates and that, because when you finally get in, they'll ask, and you'll forget. Everyone forgets in the room.
Tracey: Right. That's useful. My sister's no help.
Chiamaka: It's always one daughter doing it, isn't it. I'm the eldest, I know. Even from Leeds I'm the one sorting everything back home in Nigeria.
Tracey: Do you get back much?
Chiamaka: About every eighteen months. Not enough, really.
Tracey: Long way, though.
Chiamaka: It is. My poor mum. Anyway! Do you go on holiday? Please say yes, I need to live through someone.
Tracey: Tenerife. Been four times. All-inclusive, sunbed, done.
Chiamaka: Tenerife! I've not done Tenerife. I did Dubai last year, and Barcelona, with my girls. Lots of dressing up, lots of photos.
Tracey: I don't do the photos. Dean takes one of me looking miserable by the pool and that's it.
Chiamaka: Ha! That's the real holiday photo, though. Mine are all fake, I'm standing there for twenty minutes.
Tracey: What d'you watch, then, after all them nights?
Chiamaka: Love Island. I'm not ashamed.
Tracey: I watch Gogglebox. Anything with people arguing, really.
Chiamaka: Yes! That's the best telly. Who's your favourite on Gogglebox?
Tracey: The ones that hate everything.
Chiamaka: Ha, of course. I think we'd get on, Tracey.
Tracey: Yeah, you're alright.

=== CALL C0577 ===
Gemma: Hi, can you hear me? I'm Gemma, Hornchurch.
Ryan: Yeah. Ryan. Castleford.
Gemma: Okay. So what do you do, Ryan?
Ryan: Mechanic. Independent garage. MOT tester an' all.
Gemma: Oh, useful. My husband's an electrician, so between us we'd be a whole trades directory. I'm a speech and language therapist.
Ryan: Right. Kids?
Gemma: Mostly children, yeah. Speech sounds, language delays. I'm self-employed.
Ryan: Fair enough.
Gemma: ...So, do you enjoy it? The garage?
Ryan: It's alright. I like the work. Don't like customers much.
Gemma: Ha. Honest. What's wrong with the customers?

Ryan: Same. Folk don't check their oil for three years then come in when it's seized.
Gemma: Exactly. That's exactly it. Erm, have you ever thought about going on your own? Self-employed?
Ryan: Bit. Mobile mechanic, maybe. Have a van. No boss.
Gemma: What's stopping you?

Ryan: Yeah. Probably.
Gemma: Sorry, I'm not having a go.
Ryan: No, it's fine. Chloe says the same.
Gemma: Chloe's your partner?
Ryan: Girlfriend. Works in a nursery.
Gemma: Well, she sounds sensible. Electric cars, is that something you'd have to learn?
Ryan: Yeah, if I wanted to stay in it long term. Garage might pay for the course. Haven't asked.
Gemma: Ask. Honestly. Worst case, they say no.
Ryan: Fair.
Gemma: What do you drive, then? Something flash, I imagine.
Ryan: Old Focus ST. Doing it up. Been waiting on a part for six week.
Gemma: Six weeks! Dean'd be climbing the walls. What's it for, the part?
Ryan: Turbo. Hard to get hold of.
Gemma: Right. I won't pretend I know what that means.
Ryan: Makes it go quicker.
Gemma: Ha. Fair enough.

=== CALL C0578 ===
Chiamaka: Hello! Oh, it's you, I was hoping I'd get you! I'm Chiamaka, in Leeds.
Joanne: Oh, hello, love! Joanne, Gosport. Were you really? That's ever so nice of you.
Chiamaka: Yes! Your picture, with the lighthouse and the little blanket on the settee, I said you look like the sweet ladies who bring biscuits onto the ward.

Joanne: I will. I'll tell my sister you said, she's always on at me. Erm, anyway, what do you do when you're not at the hospital?

Chiamaka: My partner, Tunde, and my cousin's staying with us, she's doing nursing. She finishes the milk every single day.
Joanne: Ha! My cat does that with his food, leaves me nothing but a dirty bowl. Biscuit. He's elderly, bless him.
Chiamaka: Biscuit! That's such a good name. Of course you have a cat called Biscuit.
Joanne: I don't know if that's very interesting, me going on about the cat.
Chiamaka: It is, it's my favourite part so far!

Shazia: Is it hard on your back, though? To be honest that's what I'm worried about.
Joanne: Erm, I won't lie to you, love, it can be. It's the standing, and the lifting the big trays out of the oven, and then wiping all the tables in the hall after. Some days I go home and I can barely get up the stairs to my flat. But our cook's good, she'll swap me onto the till or the salad bit if I'm struggling. It depends on the school, really. I'd say ask them what the actual jobs are before you start. Sorry, I don't want to put you off.
Shazia: No, that's helpful. Better you say it.
Joanne: Have you got your food hygiene? That's the first thing they ask.

Joanne: Well, there you go, you're halfway there already.

Joanne: Every afternoon?
Shazia: Most. She's alright. She just sits there and tells me how to do things, d'you know what I mean.
Joanne: Oh dear. Ha. My mum used to do that, God rest her. She'd stand at my cooker going "you want more salt in that".
Shazia: Yeah. That's her.
Joanne: Do you get a bit of time for yourself at all?
Shazia: Dramas. Pakistani dramas on YouTube, at night. I'm hooked on one now, she's just found out her husband's been lying about everything.
Joanne: Oh, I love a drama! I'm all crime ones and The Chase. And I do a bit of crochet, little hats for the baby unit at the hospital.
Shazia: That's nice, that.
Joanne: Thank you, love. I don't know if that's very interesting.
Shazia: It is. More useful than me watching YouTube.
Joanne: Oh no, we all need our telly. What do they eat at your house for a treat, then?
Shazia: Chips from the chippy on a Friday, in a bap. Hamza won't have it any other way.
Joanne: Friday fish and chips, same as me!
calls.C0576:
Chiamaka: Hello hello! Can you hear me okay? I'm Chiamaka, in Leeds.
Tracey: Yeah. Tracey. Sittingbourne, in Kent.
Chiamaka: Kent! The garden of England, they call it, right? So what do you do, Tracey?
Tracey: Shelf stacking. Early mornings at a supermarket. What about you, you're a nurse or something? I saw the top.
Chiamaka: Doctor, actually! Acute medicine. But honestly, the nurses run the place, I just get the credit, ha. I've just come off four nights so I'm a bit loopy.
Tracey: Four nights. I'm up at quarter past four and I moan about it.
Chiamaka: No, quarter past four is a proper night shift, that counts! You're on your feet the whole time as well, lifting, everything.
Tracey: Yeah. Quicker than most of them, to be honest. I just want it done so I can go home at eleven.
Chiamaka: I love that. Get in, get it done, go home. I wish I could do that, but there's always one more discharge summary.
Tracey: Can I ask you something, since you're a doctor?
Chiamaka: Go on, everyone does! My whole family WhatsApp asks me.
Tracey: My mum's getting forgetful. Like, leaving the gas on, asking the same thing three times. She's had the memory test at the GP and they've referred her, but it's been months. Is that normal, the wait?
Chiamaka: Erm. Honestly? Yeah, the memory clinic waits are long, it's not just you. What I'd say is, if something happens, like a fall, or she gets suddenly confused, really suddenly, over a day or two, that's different, that can be an infection, and you get her seen quickly. Don't wait on the clinic for that. And keep a little list of what you notice, dates and that, because when you finally get in, they'll ask, and you'll forget. Everyone forgets in the room.
Tracey: Right. That's useful. My sister's no help.
Chiamaka: It's always one daughter doing it, isn't it. I'm the eldest, I know. Even from Leeds I'm the one sorting everything back home in Nigeria.
Tracey: Do you get back much?
Chiamaka: About every eighteen months. Not enough, really.
Tracey: Long way, though.
Chiamaka: It is. My poor mum. Anyway! Do you go on holiday? Please say yes, I need to live through someone.
Tracey: Tenerife. Been four times. All-inclusive, sunbed, done.
Chiamaka: Tenerife! I've not done Tenerife. I did Dubai last year, and Barcelona, with my girls. Lots of dressing up, lots of photos.
Tracey: I don't do the photos. Dean takes one of me looking miserable by the pool and that's it.
Chiamaka: Ha! That's the real holiday photo, though. Mine are all fake, I'm standing there for twenty minutes.
Tracey: What d'you watch, then, after all them nights?
Chiamaka: Love Island. I'm not ashamed.
Tracey: I watch Gogglebox. Anything with people arguing, really.
Chiamaka: Yes! That's the best telly. Who's your favourite on Gogglebox?
Tracey: The ones that hate everything.
Chiamaka: Ha, of course. I think we'd get on, Tracey.
Tracey: Yeah, you're alright.
calls.C0577:
Gemma: Hi, can you hear me? I'm Gemma, Hornchurch.
Ryan: Yeah. Ryan. Castleford.
Gemma: Okay. So what do you do, Ryan?
Ryan: Mechanic. Independent garage. MOT tester an' all.
Gemma: Oh, useful. My husband's an electrician, so between us we'd be a whole trades directory. I'm a speech and language therapist.
Ryan: Right. Kids?
Gemma: Mostly children, yeah. Speech sounds, language delays. I'm self-employed.
Ryan: Fair enough.
Gemma: ...So, do you enjoy it? The garage?
Ryan: It's alright. I like the work. Don't like customers much.
Gemma: Ha. Honest. What's wrong with the customers?
Ryan: People argue about the quote. They think you're making it up. You show 'em the worn pads and they still say it's too much. I'd rather just be under the car.
Gemma: See, I get that, actually. I get parents who argue about my rates, and I've got ten years in the NHS behind me. I know what I'm worth. And then they don't do the home practice and wonder why nothing's changed.
Ryan: Same. Folk don't check their oil for three years then come in when it's seized.
Gemma: Exactly. That's exactly it. Erm, have you ever thought about going on your own? Self-employed?
Ryan: Bit. Mobile mechanic, maybe. Have a van. No boss.
Gemma: What's stopping you?
Ryan: Dunno. Money. Getting the van. Getting round to it.
Gemma: Sorry, can I be blunt? "Getting round to it" isn't really a reason. You need a plan. Costs, how many jobs a week you'd need, whether you'd keep some hours at the garage at first. That's what I did. I had a spreadsheet before I handed my notice in.
Ryan: Yeah. Probably.
Gemma: Sorry, I'm not having a go.
Ryan: No, it's fine. Chloe says the same.
Gemma: Chloe's your partner?
Ryan: Girlfriend. Works in a nursery.
Gemma: Well, she sounds sensible. Electric cars, is that something you'd have to learn?
Ryan: Yeah, if I wanted to stay in it long term. Garage might pay for the course. Haven't asked.
Gemma: Ask. Honestly. Worst case, they say no.
Ryan: Fair.
Gemma: What do you drive, then? Something flash, I imagine.
Ryan: Old Focus ST. Doing it up. Been waiting on a part for six week.
Gemma: Six weeks! Dean'd be climbing the walls. What's it for, the part?
Ryan: Turbo. Hard to get hold of.
Gemma: Right. I won't pretend I know what that means.
Ryan: Makes it go quicker.
Gemma: Ha. Fair enough.
calls.C0578:
Chiamaka: Hello! Oh, it's you, I was hoping I'd get you! I'm Chiamaka, in Leeds.
Joanne: Oh, hello, love! Joanne, Gosport. Were you really? That's ever so nice of you.
Chiamaka: Yes! Your picture, with the lighthouse and the little blanket on the settee, I said you look like the sweet ladies who bring biscuits onto the ward.
Joanne: Ha! Well, I'm not a biscuit lady, I'm a cake lady. Victoria sponge, for birthdays. Sorry, are you a nurse, love? I saw your top.
Chiamaka: Doctor. Acute medicine. I've just done four nights, so excuse my face.
Joanne: Oh, you poor thing, you must be shattered. You look lovely, though, honestly, you've got such a smile.
Chiamaka: Stop, you'll make me cry, I'm too tired for compliments! What do you do, Joanne?
Joanne: I'm a kitchen assistant at a primary school. Eleven years. Erm, I do the prep, serve at lunch, wash up, all that. I know all the little ones, which ones have allergies and that. I'm a bit like you, really, only with fish fingers instead of patients.
Chiamaka: No, that's important! Allergies? That's life and death, that's basically medicine.
Joanne: Oh, I don't know about that, but thank you. Erm, can I ask you something? You can say no.
Chiamaka: Go on, everybody asks me things. My whole family WhatsApp.
Joanne: It's my knees, and my chest. I've got arthritis and asthma, and the cold mornings, I'm sort of wheezing by the time I get to work. I don't like to bother the GP, they're so busy, but I've had a couple of days off lately and I feel awful letting the cook down.
Chiamaka: Okay, listen to me, love. You are not bothering anybody. If your asthma's worse in the cold and you're needing your inhaler more, that's exactly what the asthma review is for, they might change what you're on. And ask about the knees too, there's physio, there's things. And please don't feel guilty about sick days. You're allowed to be a person.
Joanne: Oh, I'm sorry, I'm going a bit wobbly. That's very kind. Thank you.
Chiamaka: No sorry! I mean it. Book the review.
Joanne: I will. I'll tell my sister you said, she's always on at me. Erm, anyway, what do you do when you're not at the hospital?
Chiamaka: Church choir! I'm an alto. We've got a big Easter service coming up and we've been practising every week. And Love Island, I won't lie to you.
Joanne: Oh, I watch Strictly with my sister on the phone, we score them ourselves. She's ever so harsh.
Chiamaka: I love that! On the phone together, that's so cute.
Joanne: Well, she's ten minutes away, but we like our own settees. Do you have a family up there?
Chiamaka: My partner, Tunde, and my cousin's staying with us, she's doing nursing. She finishes the milk every single day.
Joanne: Ha! My cat does that with his food, leaves me nothing but a dirty bowl. Biscuit. He's elderly, bless him.
Chiamaka: Biscuit! That's such a good name. Of course you have a cat called Biscuit.
Joanne: I don't know if that's very interesting, me going on about the cat.
Chiamaka: It is, it's my favourite part so far!
calls.C0579:

Tracey: Alright. Tracey, Sittingbourne.

Ryan: Yeah. Who said?

Tracey: Do you like it, the garage?

Ryan: Ha. Yeah.
Tracey: Got a dog? You look like a dog person.

calls.C0581:
Joanne: Hello, love, can you hear me? Sorry, I always say that. I'm Joanne, I'm in Gosport.
Gemma: Yes, I can hear you fine. Gemma, Hornchurch. You've got it working, then.
Joanne: Just about! My sister set it up on the phone for me. Erm, what do you do, Gemma? I had you down as a teacher from your picture.
Gemma: Close. Speech and language therapist. Mostly children, self-employed. I did ten years in the NHS first.
Joanne: Oh, that's clever. I'm only in a school kitchen. A primary. Eleven years now.
Gemma: Don't say "only". My mum did school dinners for years in Dagenham. She used to come home with her hands red raw from the big sinks. It's proper hard work.
Joanne: Oh, did she? Ah, bless her. It is, it's the standing that does me. And the lifting the trays. My knees and my back aren't what they was, and I've had a couple of days off lately, and I feel terrible, 'cause the cook's relying on me.
Gemma: Have you said anything to the school? About maybe doing less of the heavy stuff?
Joanne: Erm, no. I worry they'd think I can't do the job, and then, you know. I can't really afford to drop my hours.
Gemma: Sorry, can I be a bit blunt? You've been there eleven years. You know every child's allergies, I'd put money on it. They're not going to want to lose you. If you go in and say "I want to keep doing this, can we adjust the lifting", that's not weakness, that's you planning. Schools have to make reasonable adjustments anyway. Write down what you'd want before you go in, so you don't get flustered.
Joanne: Oh. I hadn't thought of it like that. I would get flustered, you're right.
Gemma: Everyone does. I reread my emails about five times before I send them.
Joanne: Do you? I'd never have guessed, you look ever so organised.
Gemma: I've heard that a lot today.
Joanne: Ha! Sorry. Erm, have you got children yourself?
Gemma: Two. Ruby's eleven, Alfie's eight. You?
Joanne: No, I never did. Just my cat, Biscuit. But I crochet little hats and blankets for the baby unit at QA, the hospital in Portsmouth. The tiny ones, for the prem babies. They're no bigger than a satsuma, some of them.
Gemma: Oh, that's lovely. Alfie was... he had a bit of a rough start. They have those knitted things on the ward. I remember thinking someone's sat and made that.
Joanne: Oh, love. I hope he's alright now?
Gemma: He's fine. He's eight and he wants a dog, so he's very much fine.
Joanne: Ha! Well, tell him a cat's less work. Biscuit just sleeps on my jigsaw.
Gemma: What are you doing at the moment?
Joanne: Thousand-piece, a harbour scene. It's a nightmare, love, it's all sky. Do you do anything like that?
Gemma: Book group. And parkrun. And redoing rooms, which Dean hates.
Joanne: Oh, I'd love to be that busy. I don't know if I've been very interesting, sorry.
Gemma: You have, actually. And book that chat with the school, yeah?
Joanne: I will. Thank you, Gemma. Thank you.

Chiamaka: Fishing! Do you catch anything?
